title: Jury rules Tabesh death a homicide
article: A five-person jury at the coroner's inquest into the death of Keyvan Tabesh, who was shot by a Port Moody police officer in 2003, classified the 18-year-old's death a homicide and issued two recommendations Friday afternoon.

After listening to testimony all week in a high-security courtroom in New Westminster Law Courts, they recommended that the Ministry of Health and Fraser Health Authority issue reminders to patients suffering from mental health problems to ensure regular checkups.

As well, the jury pointed the finger at police departments in B.C., recommending the province's solicitor general, the head of the RCMP's E Division, the Association of Municipal Chiefs of Police of B.C. and Port Moody Police Department Chief Const. Paul Shrive fit all police vehicles with emergency equipment -- the very least of which should be portable "fireballs," or lights that can attach to a vehicle's dash.

In the reasons for judgment, after offering the jury's collective sympathies to the Tabesh family and the constable involved, the foreman told the inquest that, "We believe the occupant of the Tabesh vehicle may have acted differently if they had known it was a police vehicle."
Tabesh's mother, Forough Jabalameli, said the jury's recommendations would have helped her son.

"The jury took their job very seriously. I appreciate it," she said outside the law courts, "but I'm surprised because I expected more recommendations regarding this homicide. But, they didn't. I don't know why. ..."
"Maybe we can come to a conclusion about what should be done in the future, and not (let) this kind of tragedy happen to the teenagers."
The Tabesh family lawyer, Don Morrison, said "the concern here is preventing it from happening to other young boys.

"(The recommendations) are helpful, they're very helpful, absolutely. I can say nothing but praise for the jury system, both in a criminal context and in the context of the inquest," Morrison said. "There's always more to be done."
The Burnaby man was killed by a bullet fired from the gun of a Port Moody police officer on July 14, 2003, as he rushed towards the detective with a machete.
A coroner's inquest took place this week to publicly ascertain what happened that night.

Shortly before 2 a.m. on July 14, 2003, two women reported that they had been attacked by a man with a machete while they were in their car outside of Sidepocket Billiards, near the intersection of Moray and St. John's streets.

They told police their vehicle had been bumped by a black Honda Prelude, and an armed man had climbed out, threatened them, smashed the rear driver's side window of the car and hit the car with the knife.
While an officer was interviewing the two women, the Prelude drove by. The officer tried to follow the car and block it in on a nearby street, but it drove away.
The officer involved in the shooting, who can't be named because of a publication ban, gave evidence at the inquest Wednesday and said he'd do the same thing again.
"I've gone over this in my mind for two years now and there's not a thing I could have done differently," he said.

The detective had been called in on a day off to take statements related to a robbery at Hilltop Market, at the top of Clarke Street. He said he went from home to the police station, where he picked up an unmarked gold Mazda Protege and went to do interviews with a briefcase, gun and portable police radio with him.
He said while he was doing interviews the radio was almost off, but when he'd finished he turned it up in time to hear Const. Darrin Conlon call for backup.
"It sounded like he was in trouble," the detective said.

As he was heading down Snake Hill at 1:30 a.m., the officer heard that a chase was heading in his direction, and decided to pull off the road because it wasn't safe to join a pursuit in an unmarked car with no emergency equipment.
He turned on to St. George Street and turned to face Clarke, in anticipation of seeing the pursuit go by.

Instead, the black Prelude, driven by Tabesh, turned on to the cul-de-sac and as it went by, the officer said he saw at least three people inside and made eye contact with the occupants, and he was certain they'd spotted him as a police officer.

He said he radioed his location, turned around, and slowly approached the Prelude, which had turned around at the end of the cul-de-sac. He pulled his car up to within inches of the Honda's front bumper with the intention of boxing the car in and preventing a further police chase.

It was then, the officer said, that someone came on the radio to warn him that the occupants of the Prelude were armed. The officer then backed his car up about two vehicle lengths to give the car's occupants a chance to escape or sit in the car and wait for other police officers to arrive.
"I realized I was not in a good position if they had weapons," he said.
Seconds later Tabesh got out of the car, machete in hand, and started towards the officer, along with a passenger of the car, Amir Aghaei, who said Tuesday that he was trying to stop his friend.
The officer said he yelled, "Police! Don't anyone move," but the pair kept coming towards him.
"There was absolutely no doubt in my mind that they were going to kill me," he said. "I realized I had no choice but to use deadly force."
He fired a shot at Tabesh, which hit the man's arm and didn't appear to slow him down, then one at Aghaei, who had run around the other side of the Mazda and was hit in the leg by the shot.
Then the officer turned back to Tabesh, who he said was within six feet of him, and fired three shots "as fast as I could get them off.
"I couldn't get them off fast enough."

Tabesh fell to the ground in front of the officer and he said that only then did he see that the weapon was a machete. He said he called for two ambulances, but knew that Tabesh was dead because of where he had been hit.
Tabesh died on the way to the hospital from a gunshot wound to the heart.

Use of force experts that gave evidence Thursday didn't criticize the officer's choices, but said there were options available. Those included staying at the other car's bumper, moving back further, not turning around and approaching the Prelude at all, or taking the action he did.

A toxicologist said that at death, Tabesh's blood alcohol level was .107, slightly above the legal limit for operating a motor vehicle. Tabesh also had a small amount of antidepressant in his body, as he was being treated for depressive, psychotic symptoms. Tabesh also reportedly had problems with anger management and dealing with authority.
John Bethell, council for the coroner, reiterated that the purpose of the inquest is to let everybody know what happened and have the recommendations.
While the inquest is over, Morrison said the family's healing has yet to begin.

"I suspect there will be no closure," he said, turning to Jabalameli. "(She is) a mother. This will go on for a long time. It's not so much closure, it's coming to peace with things in a way. It's really too early to even come to peace."
